summary: Specifies version 3 of the RFC Editor Model. Policy definition becomes the joint responsibility of the RFC Series Working Group, which proposes policy, and the RFC Series Approval Board, which approves it. Policy implementation is mainly the job of the RFC Production Center. It obsoletes RFC 8728 and was later replaced by RFC 9920.

eli5.summary: The group that publishes the RFCs had a rulebook for who does what. This version splits making the rules from carrying them out, with different groups for each.

questions: who is responsible for the rfc series
what is the rfc editor model
what does the rfc production center do
subtitle: Who writes the rules for the RFC Series, who approves them, and who publishes the documents.

tldr.problem: Versions 1 and 2 of the RFC Editor Model left the community with a lack of transparency, few avenues for input into policy, and unclear lines of authority and responsibility.
tldr.mechanism: Policy definition is split between the open RFC Series Working Group (RSWG), which proposes policy, and the RFC Series Approval Board (RSAB), which approves it, while policy implementation sits mainly with the RFC Production Center (RPC) under contract oversight by the IETF LLC.
tldr.outcome: It obsoleted RFC 8728 and created the Editorial Stream, but it was itself obsoleted by RFC 9920 and updated by RFC 9720.

facts.label: RSAB approval vote
facts.value: At least three voting members vote YES

today: RFC 9280 is obsoleted by RFC 9920 and was updated by RFC 9720, so check those for the current model. It obsoleted RFC 8728.

sections.title: The Model in Brief
sections.content:
The RFC Series is the archival series for Internet technical specifications, published continually since 1969. RFCs come from several document streams. Each stream approving body is responsible for the content of its stream, while the RFC Editor function is responsible for production and distribution of all RFCs.

Version 3 of the model divides the work into two tasks. Policy definition for the Series as a whole is the joint job of the RFC Series Working Group (RSWG), an open working group independent of the IETF that generates proposals, and the RFC Series Approval Board (RSAB), an appointed body that approves them. Policy implementation is mainly the job of the RFC Production Center (RPC), which is contractually overseen by the IETF Administration LLC (IETF LLC). The RFC Series Consulting Editor (RSCE) gives expert advice to the RPC and RSAB.

The RFC obsoletes RFC 8728, updates RFC 7841 by defining boilerplate for a new stream, updates RFC 8729 by replacing the RFC Editor role with the RSWG, RSAB and RSCE, and updates RFC 8730.
sections.eli5: One group suggests rules, another group says yes or no, and a publishing team does the daily work. A helper with publishing know-how advises both.

sections.title: Defining Policy: RSWG and RSAB
sections.content:
Everyone interested may take part in the RSWG. It has two chairs, one appointed by the IESG and one by the IAB, and it works by rough consensus in a way similar to IETF working groups, with open meetings and a publicly archived discussion list.

The RSAB may only review policy proposals from the RSWG; it has no independent authority to formulate policy. Its voting members are one representative each for the IETF, IAB, IRTF and Independent Streams, plus the RSCE. The IETF Executive Director (or a delegate) and an RPC representative are non-voting ex officio members. The RSAB keeps a public record of its proceedings.

A proposal must be submitted to and adopted by the RSWG, pass a Last Call in the working group and a community call for comments, and be approved by the RSAB. Policies may cover things like document formats, publication processes and overall management of the Series.
sections.eli5: Anyone can suggest a rule in the open group. A small board of stream representatives checks it and can only say yes or send it back, never write rules on its own.

sections.title: The Policy Workflow
sections.content:
A proposal begins as an Internet-Draft and is adopted if the chairs find rough consensus. After discussion, the chairs issue a Last Call in the working group. Once they find consensus, the RSAB issues a community call for comments, which lasts not less than two weeks, and also considers the proposal itself.

The RSAB then polls its members. Each position is YES, CONCERN or RECUSE. A CONCERN must be explained to the community and is allowed for three reasons: a serious problem for one or more streams, serious harm to the Series, or lack of rough consensus after the community call. A proposal without any CONCERN is approved. If any remain, the RSAB votes, and at least three voting members must vote YES. If not approved, the proposal goes back to the RSWG. Approved documents are published as Informational RFCs in the Editorial Stream, and policies may take effect before publication.

Appeals against RSWG chair decisions go to the RSAB and appeals against RSAB decisions go to the IAB, on grounds of failure to follow the correct process, generally within thirty (30) days.
sections.eli5: A rule idea gets talked over, then the whole community is asked what it thinks, and finally the board votes. If a worried board member remains, three yes votes are still enough.

sections.title: Publishing: The RPC, RSCE and IETF LLC
sections.content:
The RPC publishes RFCs from all streams. Its responsibilities include editing documents against the RFC Style Guide, keeping records of edits and author dialogue, coordinating with IANA, assigning RFC numbers, publishing and providing online access to RFCs, running the errata system and preserving records. The RPC is advised by the RSCE and RSAB, and it must tell the RSAB if it decides against their advice.

The IETF LLC oversees the RPC, negotiates its performance targets, and runs vendor selection and the budget. The model does not fix whether the RPC is a separate company under contract, employees, or contractors.

The RSCE is a senior technical publishing professional who is a voting RSAB member, spots problems and improvements in the publication process, and gives expert advice to the RSWG, RPC and IETF LLC. The IETF LLC selects and evaluates the RSCE using a selection committee.

If authors and the RPC disagree, they first consult directly. Stream-specific conflicts involve the relevant stream approving body, cross-stream conflicts involve the RSAB, and new issues are resolved by the RSAB, which also brings them to the RSWG for a new policy.
sections.eli5: The publishing team edits and releases every document, and keeps the records safe. If an author and the editors disagree, they talk first, then ask the right group for help.

sections.title: The Editorial Stream and Changes from Version 2
sections.content:
This document creates the Editorial Stream as a separate space for policies, procedures, guidelines and rules about the RFC Series as a whole. All documents produced by the RSWG and approved by the RSAB are published there with a status of Informational. The stream cannot publish Standards Track or Best Current Practice RFCs, which are reserved for the IETF Stream.

Version 1 was RFC 5620 and version 2 was RFC 6635, modified in 2020 by RFC 8728. The community found problems with a lack of transparency, a lack of avenues for input into policy definition, and unclear lines of authority. In 2020 the IAB formed the RFC Editor Future Development Program to address them. As a result, the RFC Series Editor's duties are split among the new bodies, the RFC Publisher role is merged into the RPC, and the RFC Series Oversight Committee (RSOC) is disbanded. The RFC Series Advisory Group (RSAG) from version 1 is affirmed to be disbanded.

The model also lists historical properties of the Series that proposals should not harm without scrutiny: availability, accessibility, English publication with translation allowed, diversity of document types, quality, stability (published documents are not changed) and longevity.
sections.eli5: There is now a special shelf for rules about the whole series. Some old committees were closed because it was too hard to tell who was in charge.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8729 apply. The publication process must prevent unapproved changes, and because several entities, especially the RPC, take part in maintaining the index of publications, enough security must exist to stop external parties from changing published documents. The archive, source documents and associated originals such as errata lists must be secured against data storage failure.

For IANA, the RPC coordinates with IANA so RFCs accurately document registries and assigned values. The document creates no registry and needs no IANA action.
sections.eli5: Published documents must be protected from sneaky edits, and backed up so they cannot be lost.

viz.caption: WHO DOES WHAT IN THE RFC EDITOR MODEL (VERSION 3)

items.title: RSWG
items.text: Open working group that proposes policies for the RFC Series.

items.title: RSAB
items.text: Appointed board that approves or returns RSWG proposals.

items.title: RPC
items.text: Edits and publishes RFCs from all streams.

items.title: RSCE
items.text: Publishing expert who advises the RPC, RSAB and RSWG.

items.title: IETF LLC
items.text: Contractually oversees the RPC and handles budget and vendor selection.
